summary:
Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1977, with an equal age of consent of 14, and the prohibition has not been restored. A trans visitor faces no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting gender non-conformingly in public.

The Law on Prohibition of Discrimination, passed on 27 July 2010, lists gender identity as a prohibited ground and reaches employment, the provision of goods and services, education and health services. Criminal Code amendments adopted in 2013 and in force from 3 June 2014 prohibit hate speech based on gender identity and provide penalty enhancements where an offence is committed because of the victim's LGBT status, gender identity included.

Those enhancements are applied unevenly. The European Commission has found that prosecutors bring misdemeanour charges where hate-crime proceedings are warranted, which limits the sentencing uplift the Criminal Code provides.

No legal gender recognition statute based on self-determination exists. Change of legal gender requires a medical diagnosis, sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, and divorce where the applicant is married. A draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity based on self-determination completed its legislative steps and consultations but was not adopted; the 2024 deadline set under the EU accession programme passed, and the law remained unadopted as of November 2025. The practical effect for a visitor is documentary: there is no administrative procedure in the country that will issue a record in an acquired gender.

The Constitution bars same-sex marriage, and households headed by same-sex couples do not receive the protections attached to opposite-sex marriage. Since 15 July 2021 same-sex couples may register a Life Partnership, approved by parliament on 1 July 2020 by 42 votes to 5, signed on 3 July 2020 and published on 7 July 2020, which carries almost all the rights of marriage except adoption, foster care and parenting. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under the country's birth-sex-based rules can have that relationship recognised only through a registration made before a registrar in the country.

Public visibility has drawn organised hostility alongside state protection. The first Pride march in Podgorica in 2013 put roughly 150 marchers on the street under a guard of some 2,000 police; opponents threw rocks and were dispersed with tear gas. The 2011 Pride had been cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital.

Official hostility has not disappeared. Anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric continued through 2023. In the same period a psychologist who appeared on television in gender-non-conforming clothes was subjected to hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, and the police response was monitored by the organisation recording the case. Over 222 online hate-speech incidents were reported.

A 2018 study by the ERA Western Balkans office found that 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted, a measure of how much hostility is absorbed privately rather than reported.
tangentialFactors:
Montenegro decriminalised in 1977 in the same year as Croatia and Slovenia, and the three are grouped as the earliest cohort in the region to repeal such provisions.

Parliamentary treatment of partnership rights has moved in both directions. A government draft in December 2018 offered near marriage-equivalent rights through a registrar ceremony while explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption. On 31 July 2019 parliament blocked the partnership bill despite government backing, with the ERA Western Balkans office describing LGBT people as forced to live as second-class citizens without hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights. The Life Partnership law was adopted the following year.

Legal gender recognition is tied to EU accession conditionality. The self-determination draft completed its legislative steps and consultations but missed its 2024 adoption deadline, and the absence of a framework free of abusive requirements is counted against the country in accession monitoring.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must obtain a medical diagnosis, undergo sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, and divorce if married. No self-determination procedure has been enacted.

The Life Partnership is registered before a registrar and grants almost the same rights as opposite-sex marriage, with adoption, foster care and parenting excluded. The Constitution bars same-sex marriage, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same protections as opposite-sex married households.

An anti-discrimination study found that only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation.

A new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with a budget of €45,000.

Gays, lesbians and bisexuals are not barred from military service.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source records how border officers or police handle a trans traveller's documents, and no screening or marker-flagging practice at Montenegrin border points is documented.

Whether a foreign gender recognition certificate is accepted for any administrative purpose in Montenegro is not addressed in the sources.

The figure of over 222 online hate-speech incidents is a count of reports, not a rate; no denominator is published.

The outcome of police monitoring of the attacks on the television psychologist is not recorded.

Whether Life Partnership registration is open to non-residents is not stated in the sources.

Incident reporting is not disaggregated for trans people, so no trans-specific violence rate with a comparable denominator is available.
